The level/rate of urbanization: the percentage of a population that is urban, and the pace at which that share rises

claims.claim: Urbanization is the process by which an increasing share of a population lives in urban areas rather than rural areas; it is measured by the level of urbanization, the percentage of a population that is urban.

The urban share of the world's population grew from a small minority in 1800 (about 3 percent) to a majority in the early 21st century; the UN's World Urbanization Prospects series marks the world passing roughly 50 percent urban around 2007-2008.
The United Nations reported that 55 percent of the world's population lived in urban areas in 2018 and projected that share to rise to about 68 percent by 2050.

The UN projected that urban areas could add about 2.5 billion people between 2018 and 2050, with close to 90 percent of that increase concentrated in Asia and Africa, and India, China, and Nigeria together accounting for over one-third of the projected growth.
A megacity is an urban agglomeration with 10 million or more inhabitants; the UN counted 33 megacities in 2018 and projected 43 by 2030, most of them in the developing world.

More-developed regions are already highly urbanized (roughly three-quarters urban) while less-developed regions have a lower urban share but are urbanizing faster; the OER reports about 78 percent urban in developed countries versus about 49 percent in developing countries as of 2017.

Urbanization is driven by rural-to-urban migration (drawn by higher wages and industrial and service jobs in cities), natural increase among urban residents, and reclassification of settlements from rural to urban as they grow.

When urban growth outpaces the supply of housing, infrastructure, and services, it can produce informal settlements and strain on basic services; managing urban growth sustainably is a policy concern raised by the UN.
What counts as 'urban' is set by each country's national definition rather than a single global standard, which affects cross-country comparisons of urbanization levels.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact year the world became majority urban depends on how 'urban' is defined.
positions: The UN's World Urbanization Prospects series, built on national definitions, dates the crossing to about 2007-2008.
Our World in Data notes that alternative density-based methods such as the EU/UN DEGURBA framework place the majority-urban crossing much earlier.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Use the widely-cited UN World Urbanization Prospects milestone of roughly 2007-2008, attribute it to the UN, and note that the figure depends on the definition of 'urban' rather than presenting it as an exact undisputed date.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was filed under the wrong subject (sociology) and treated 'urbanization' as an abstract organizing 'concept' with no geographic content, definitions, drivers, or data.
The draft's vocabulary defined 'Urbanization' circularly as 'a foundational Sociology concept covered in this lesson.'
